Every padel group makes the same mistake. It is such an easy one to make.

A group in Rotterdam kept organising single evenings, and kept losing people in between them.

Every few weeks somebody proposed a match. Four players were needed, six got asked, and the two who missed out were a little less likely to answer the next message. Nobody meant anything by it. It just adds up.

The mistake was treating padel as a series of evenings instead of something with a shape. There was nothing to be part of. There were only invitations to accept or decline.

What worked was picking a format. That is really all it took.

EffePadelle has two, and they are genuinely different things. Pick the one that fits your group, or run both.

A CASUAL COMPETITION runs for weeks or months. Everyone plays everyone once, at your own pace. There is no end date and no pressure. You book each match whenever it suits the two of you, and your calendars find the evening for you. This is the one for a group that plays most weeks and wants a table that actually means something by the end.

A ONE DAY TOURNAMENT is finished in one afternoon. Everybody plays on the same day. It works with 4 of you and it works with 28 people across five courts. The app plans every rotation and tells everyone which court to walk to, and a timer with a buzzer keeps the whole thing running on time. Nobody stands there with a pen and paper.

The app asks which one you want in the very first step, and everything after follows from your answer.

Both keep a leaderboard. Both let you type in a score in five seconds, with your opponent tapping to confirm. Both are free, with no trial and no catch.

That group now runs a casual competition through the winter and one big day tournament in June, which is the closest they have ever come to a tradition.

So stop asking six people for Thursday. Pick a format instead.

Search EffePadelle in the App Store or on Google Play.

Most padel groups fall apart after three weeks. Here is what actually goes wrong.

Eight colleagues in Utrecht started a padel group in January. By February there were three left. Nobody quit and nobody argued. The group ran on whoever answered the message that week, and it was always the same three.

What fixed it was giving them a season instead of loose evenings. In EffePadelle that is a CASUAL COMPETITION: everyone plays everyone once, over weeks or months, at your own pace. A table makes it obvious who has not played yet, and the rounds arrive without anyone chasing them.

Setting it up takes under a minute. It works with nine people too, so one person rests per round and nobody sits out twice in a row. Someone adds a few dates, everyone taps their availability or links their calendar, and every slot shows how many of you can make it. Each match has its own chat, so planning and booking stay in one place.

All eight are still in it. Two have never won a match and show up anyway.

It is free. A CASUAL COMPETITION runs for months, a ONE DAY TOURNAMENT is done in an afternoon, and you can run both.

Tag the one in your group who always answers.

Search EffePadelle in the App Store or on Google Play.

The police officers.

The first of three films from our fictional AI campaign. We wrote the script the way we'd write one for a shoot. Every frame after that was made with AI.

That doesn't mean you type a sentence and this comes out. You need to know what you're after and how to ask for it, and then you still throw most of it away.
